claims.text: Bidriware is a metal craft of Bidar in which designs engraved on a cast zinc-copper alloy are inlaid with silver.

quotes.quote: Bidri ware is a famous handicraft of Bidar District.
Bidriware is an alloy ofzinc , copper and other non ferrous metals. Pretty designs are engtaved on it and there after inlaid with pure silver ware.
The technique consists of casting objects from a high-zinc alloy and then inlaying them with silver or brass, or a combination of both.

claims.text: Bidri takes its name from the city of Bidar, where the technique is thought to have originated.

quotes.quote: The technique takes its name from the city of Bidar, in present day Karnataka, where it is thought to have originated
The art with silver is called Bidriware-so called after the name of the old city of Bidar
The very name "Bidri' is derived from Bidar

claims.text: Bidriware is a kind of damascene work, a system of ornamentation that encrusts one metal on another.

quotes.quote: The craft ofBidriware is a kind of damascene work.
It is a system of orna mentation consisting of encrusting one metal on the other.
Bidriware is a special type of work called Damascening in silver.

claims.text: The black background of bidri ware contrasts strikingly with its lustrous silver inlay.

quotes.quote: The contrast between the black oxidized background and lustrous silver inlay gives a beauty to the Bidri ware.
The inlays contrast strikingly with the matt black patina of the vessel.

claims.text: Bidri is a metalworking technique known only in the Indian subcontinent.

quotes.quote: Bidri is a technique known only in the Indian subcontinent
This metalwork as well as the technique to produce it are found in India alone.

claims.text: Bidar and Hyderabad are named as the chief, and in one account the only, present-day centres of bidri production.

quotes.quote: Bidar remains one of the chief centres of bidriware production in the country, alongside Hyderabad in present-day Telangana.
Today, Bidri is produced only in two centres in India: Bidar and Hyderabad.

claims.text: The GI application states that bidri was introduced in Bidar about 400 years ago by King Ahmed Shah Wali Bhamani.

quotes.quote: It was introduced in Bidar about 400 years ago by King Ahmed Shah Wali Bhamani.

claims.text: The start of bidri at Bidar is attributed to the reign of Ahmed Shah Bahamani, who ruled from 1422 to 1436.

quotes.quote: Its name is derived from Bidar where the skill in this art was developed during time of Ahmed Shah Bahamani (1422 A.D.- 1436 A.D)
The history of bidriware is said to have begun with the reign of Ahmed Shah Al Wali Baihmani.
Ahmed Shah Al Wali Baihmani (1422-1436), the ninth king of the Baihmani dynasty ruled for a period of 13 years and was a great patron of the arts.

claims.text: Citing the Karnataka Gazetteer, the GI application says Ahmed Shah Bahamani set up a training centre for Bidri workers at Bidar.

quotes.quote: As Per Karnataka Gazetteer, - Govemment of Kamataka - Bidar district, - Bidriware is a special type of work called Damascening in silver.
this sultan who was a lover of art and literature had set up a training center for Bidri workers at Bidar.

claims.text: The origin of bidri is usually attributed to the Bahamani sultans of Bidar, and the craft is dated back to the fifteenth century.

quotes.quote: The origin of Bidriware is usually attributed to the Bahamani sultans who ruled Bidar in the 14th-15th centuries.
Bidri handicraft in India, patronised by Bahamani kings, dates back to the fifteenth century

claims.text: Production of bidri in Bidar is believed to have begun under Alauddin Ahmad Bahmani II (r. 1436-58).

quotes.quote: The production of bidriware in Bidar is believed to have begun during the reign of Alauddin Ahmad Bahmani II (r. 1436-58)

claims.text: A craftsman's account in the census monograph says Allauddin II of Bidar invited the craftsmen of Bijapur to settle at Bidar.

quotes.quote: It is gathered from the narration of Bn experienced craftsman llS follows.
The beautiful articles presented to Al1auddin II (1434-1457 A. D.) of Bidar on the occasion ofhiscoro nation impressed him very much and he invited the craftsmen of Bijapur to settle at Bidar itself.
who encouraged artisans from Bijapur to settle in the capital

claims.text: A craftsman's account in the census monograph says the craft was brought to India about 900 years ago by migrants from Iraq, and its original home seems to be Iran.

quotes.quote: It is gathered from the narration of Bn experienced craftsman llS follows.
Sometime about 900 years ago the craft was brought down to India by migrants from Iraq. The original home of the work seems to be Iran

claims.text: The technique is believed to have been introduced by Persian and Syrian artisans who migrated to the Deccan under the patronage of the Bahmani sultans.

quotes.quote: The technique is believed to have been introduced to the subcontinent by Persian and Syrian artisans who migrated to the Deccan region under the patronage of the Bahmani sultans.

claims.text: A craftsman's account in the census monograph says Abdullah-bin-Khaiser, versed in the art, settled at Bijapur, and it is said that the carpenter Sivanna became the first native of India to learn it.

quotes.quote: After many years one Abdullah-bin-Khaiser, who W<lS conver sant with the knowledge of this art came down to Bijapur and settled there.
It is said that a carpenter by na'11e Sivanna, who won recognition for his services and gained confi dence of Khaiser, was taught the craft.
Thus Sivanna became the first native of India to learn this art.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis says Abdullah bin Kaiser, a craftsman from Iran, was invited by Sultan Ahmed Shah Bahmani to decorate the royal palaces and courts.

quotes.quote: Abdullah bin Kaiser, a craftsman from Iran was invited by the Sultan Ahmed Shah Bahmani to work on decorating the royal palaces and courts.

claims.text: Bidri vessels have been made in India from at least the 17th century until the present day.

quotes.quote: Bidri vessels have been manufactured in India from at least the 17th century until the present day
produced in India from the 17th century or earlier and which is still being made today

claims.text: The V&A states that bidri's origins are unknown but that surviving pieces date from the late 16th or early 17th century.

quotes.quote: Its origins are unknown, but surviving pieces date from the late 16th or early 17th century.

claims.text: Another V&A record dates the earliest bidri pieces to the early 17th century, when production is thought to have been only in centres such as Bidar and Hyderabad.

quotes.quote: The earliest pieces of bidri date from the early 17th century, when production is thought to have been only in centres such as Bidar and Hyderadabad in the Deccan sultanates.

claims.text: The Impart encyclopedia names a Deccani painting of about 1625, showing a bidri hookah, as the earliest evidence of a bidri object.

quotes.quote: The earliest evidence of a bidriware object comes from a Deccani painting dated to c. 1625, in which an officer of African descent is seen smoking a hookah made in the bidri technique.

claims.text: Sahapedia notes that no examples of bidri dating to the 15th or 16th centuries have been found in paintings or literature.

quotes.quote: No examples of bidri dating to the 15th or 16th centuries have been found in paintings or literature, thus making one sceptical if bidri should still be related to the 15th century or not.

claims.text: Jagdish Mittal identifies the earliest written reference to bidri ware in Chahar Gulshan, a Persian history of India written in 1759.

quotes.quote: The earliest reference of bidri ware is in Chahar Gulshan, a history of India written in Persian in 1759, which in turn is based on a work of 1720

claims.text: By the late eighteenth century bidri had spread to the courts of Purnia and Murshidabad, and by the nineteenth century to Lucknow.

quotes.quote: By the late eighteenth century, the technique had spread to the Muslim courts of Purnia (in present-day Bihar) and Murshidabad (in present-day Bengal), and by the nineteenth century, to Lucknow (in present-day Uttar Pradesh).

claims.text: The census monograph says the craft's popularity led to working centres at Murshidabad in Bengal, Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh and Purnia in Bihar.

quotes.quote: It gained such popularity that working centres came to be opent'd at Murshidabad in Bengal, Lucknow in Uttar Pn,desh and Purniah in Bihar.

claims.text: Sahapedia dates the start of bidri production in Lucknow, Purnea and Murshidabad to the early 19th century.

quotes.quote: By the early 19th century, bidri started to be produced in other parts of India-Lucknow, Purnea and Murshidabad.

claims.text: The technique flourished in Bidar and Hyderabad between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries and appeared regularly in Deccan paintings from the seventeenth century.

quotes.quote: The technique flourished in Bidar and Hyderabad between the sixteenth and nineteenth century and regularly appeared in Deccan paintings from the seventeenth century onwards.

claims.text: Bidriware from the Deccan was exported to the Mughal court, the Rajput courts of Rajasthan and the Maratha kingdoms.

quotes.quote: Bidriware from the region was also exported to the Mughal court, Rajput courts of Rajasthan and Maratha kingdoms.

claims.text: Bidri was extensively patronised by the Asaf Jahi dynasty, under whose rulers the industry flourished from the early 18th to the mid-20th century.

quotes.quote: The art form was also extensively patronised by the Asaf Jahi Dynasty that ruled over the Hyderabad State between the eighteenth and twentieth century.
From the early 18th century to the mid-20th century, the bidri industry flourished under the Asaf Jahi rulers.

claims.text: Many artisans from Bidar migrated to Hyderabad, the new capital of the Deccan, where the art began to flourish.

quotes.quote: Many artisans from Bidar migrated to Hyderabad, which was the new capital of the Deccan. The art started to flourish in Hyderabad.

claims.text: After the 1956 reorganisation of states placed Bidar in Mysore State, many bidri artisans migrated to Hyderabad City in 1956 and 1957.

quotes.quote: At the time of Re-organisation of States in the year 1956 Bidar was included in Mysore State.
So, many of them chose to migrate to Hyderabad City and came there in the years 1956 and 1957.
Most artisans moved to Hyderabad in search of better livelihoods as it remained a hub for trade.

claims.text: The census monograph says almost all the workers of the Hyderabad co-operative societies came originally from Bidar in pursuit of their livelihood.

quotes.quote: Almo t all the workers belong to Bidar originally and have come away to the City in pursuit of their livelihood.
The present volume consists of the monographs on (i) Bidriware of Hyderabad City

claims.text: Bidriware was exhibited at the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London, the Exposition Universelle of 1855 in Paris and the Delhi Durbar of 1903.

quotes.quote: Bidriware was exhibited at colonial exhibitions, including the Great Exhibition of 1851, the Exposition Universelle in 1855 and the Delhi Durbar of 1903.
The Great Exhibition at the Crystal Palace in London in 1851 followed by the Paris Universal Exposition, 1855 had showcased bidri.

claims.text: The international exhibitions stimulated demand and new production centres, which led to repetitious designs and inferior quality.

quotes.quote: The exhibitions stimulated demand considerably and caused new centres of production to spring up in the Indian subcontinent, but this led to repetitious designs and inferior quality as the craftsmen struggled to keep up with their markets.
This led to new production centres being established.

claims.text: There is recorded evidence that the craft declined during the later part of the 19th century.

quotes.quote: There is recorded evidence that the craft declined during the later part of the 19th century.
The bidri industry saw its first downfall in the 19th century.

claims.text: In 1817 Benjamin Heyne noted that bidri work at Bidar, once the means of enriching the place, scarcely yielded food for the five families that remained.

quotes.quote: Stronge also mentions a short note on the industry at Bidar from the Asiatic Journal, III, March 1817, in which Benjamin Heyne notes that

complained of want, in employment in which former times had been the means of substituting a numerous classis of their own cast [sic], and of enriching the place, but now scarcely yielded food for five families that remained

claims.text: Francis Buchanan, observing bidri making at Purnea in 1809-10, found each stage of the work done by a specialised set of workers.

quotes.quote: Susan Stronge mentions a well-observed description of the process of making bidri, as seen by Francis Buchanan in 1809-10 at Purnea
Each stage of the work at Purnea was done by a specialised set of workers, the object passing from one hand to another through different processes.

claims.text: The census monograph says boys trained at the beginning of the twentieth century in a school organised at Bidar, where the bidri masters Ramanna and Irsangu were instructors.

quotes.quote: Collector of Bidar and some other notable personalities took steps to bring together the talent and improve it.
A school was organised to teach this craft to young and enthusiastic boys. Ramanna and Irs<lngu were the instructors for training the boys
Among the people who received training in the school run by Ramanlla and Irsangu at the beginning of this century were the following who won reputation

claims.text: Jagdish Mittal writes that the Nizam's government started a training school for bidri at Bidar in 1931, merged with the local high school in 1938.

quotes.quote: in 1931 the Nizam's government started a training school for bidri works in 1931 at Bidar with these artisans as instructors. The school was merged with the local High School in 1938

claims.text: Susan Stronge writes that from 1950 the government trained bidri workers, its Artisans Training Institute giving hereditary workers two years of training with a monthly allowance.

quotes.quote: in 1950, special units were set up and the Government began to involve itself in training the bidri workers. The Government Artisans Training Institute provided two years training to hereditary bidri workers, giving them a monthly allowance

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis says the craft has been handed down through generations mostly among the local Muslim and Lingayat communities.

quotes.quote: Since then, the craft has been handed down succeeding generations mostly among the local Muslim and Lingayat sects.

claims.text: Sahapedia names M. A. Rauf, Shah Rasheed Ahmed Quadri and Raj Nageshwar among Bidar's award-winning bidri artisans, Rauf and Quadri as National and Shilp Guru awardees.

quotes.quote: Currently in Bidar, the artisans can be categorised into two classes-the first being the National/State/Shilp Guru Award winners versus the rest of the artisans.
This came forth after a conversation with M.A. Rauf (a National and Shilp Guru award winner)
A similar response was received from Shah Rasheed Ahmed Quadri (Senior National award and Shilp Guru award winner), Raj Nageshwar (National Award winner)

claims.text: The GI application gives Bidar district as the geographical area of production of Bidriware, made in Bidar town.

quotes.quote: (h) Geographical area of Production and Map : Bidar District
Bidar Town in Bidar District (Kamataka).

claims.text: The GI application states that Bidar is the only district in the state engaged in the craft.

quotes.quote: Bidar is the only district in the state which is engaged in this craft.

claims.text: The GI registry records Karnataka as the geographical area of the Bidriware geographical indication.

quotes.quote: | Geographical Area | Karnataka |

claims.text: Because Bidar fort is a heritage conservation site, the craft's dependence on its clay threatens its continued practice.

quotes.quote: the handicraft mandates the use of Bidar Fort (in Karnataka, India) clay, which bestows the handicraft its characteristic matt-black patina
The fort is a heritage conservation site and thus poses a threat to the perennial practice of handicraft.
Also the fort being an heritage center, an alternative to the sand has to be developed.

claims.text: The GI application's method of production runs from melting and casting the alloy through smoothing, temporary blackening, engraving, silver inlay and sanding to dipping in fort earth solution, drying and oiling.

quotes.quote: Firstly, copper and zinc are melted in the proportion of I to 16 in a crucible and the alloy is prepared. This alloy is casted with the help of molding boxes to the required pattem of article to be produced.
After casting, the surface ofthe articles is made smooth with the help of buffing machines. The smooth surface is made black temporarily by applying copper sulphate.

On the black-colour surface, the design is engraved with a grooving chisel. A pure silver wire is inlayed in the grooved portion i.e., damascening in silver and the whole surface is again rubbed with sand paper or buffrng machine.
The polished article is then dipped in a boiled solution of ammonium chloride and earth collected and available only from the fort area
The article is taken out from the solution and dried for five to ten minutes. Later the whole surface is rubbed with groundnut oil, so as to give the article a shining.

claims.text: The GI application divides bidri production into three parts: casting, engraving and inlaying.

quotes.quote: The process of production may be broadly divided into three parts vrz., casting, engraving and inlaying.

claims.text: The census monograph divides production into three phases: mould making and casting, engraving and inlaying, and finishing.

quotes.quote: The entire technique of production can be divided into three broad phases as follows: I. Mould making and casting
II. Engraving and inlaying: The design is drawn with free hand drawing on the surface
Ill. Finishing: The article is blackened and then polished carefully.

claims.text: Rolla and colleagues announce four stages of bidri operations but list three: moulding or casting, carving and inlaying, and oxidising and finishing.

quotes.quote: Broadly, the operations of Bidri handicraft are divided into four categorical stages: a) Molding (casting), b) Carving and Inlaying, c) Oxidizing and Finishing.

claims.text: One bidri artisan told The News Minute that Bidriware goes through an 8-stage process before it attains its final shape.

quotes.quote: explains Khwaja, a Bidri artisan
said that Bidriware goes through an 8-stage process before it attains its final shape.

claims.text: The alloy is melted in a crucible in a furnace that uses coal, the zinc first and the copper then added to it.

quotes.quote: the alloy metal is being melted in the furnace nearby in a crucible
First the zinc is well melted in the crucible and then the copper is added to it.
The coal used for the furnace is the burnt out railway coal ejected by the locomotives

claims.text: Moulds are made in hollow iron frames called darza boxes, with a thin layer of fine red clay mixed with resin and castor oil over the pattern and ordinary red clay filling the rest.

quotes.quote: There are hollow frames made of iron sheets which are called darza boxes.
The fine screened red clay wi th resin and castor oil mixed in it is now laid in a thin layer on the pattern plate
Over this layer, layers of ordinary red clay are laid one after the other till the whole darza box is completely filled in.

claims.text: Fine clay with resin and castor oil gives the casting a smooth surface and avoids cracks that may form if only dry clay is used.

quotes.quote: The reason for using this fine clay is to get smooth surface in the cast article and secondly to avoid cracks which may form if only dry clay is used.

claims.text: Sangjeera, a white stone powder, is dusted on the pattern so that the clay does not stick to it, and on the mould to keep it free from clay residue.

quotes.quote: Sangjeera (white stone powder)
Sangjeera powder, which is earlier tied up in a piece of cloth, is dusted on the zinc sheet including the pattern plate
This pre vents the clay from sticking on to the pattern
the resulting mould is dusted with sangjeera to keep it free from any clay residue

claims.text: Hollow objects such as vases can be cast in two pieces and soldered at a later stage.

quotes.quote: For hollow objects such as vases, the object can be cast in two pieces and soldered at a later stage.

claims.text: The cast article is smoothed to shape on a lathe and with files, or with buffing machines.

quotes.quote: The cast article is now smoothened to the desired shape and fineness with the lathe machine and also with files.
After casting, the surface ofthe articles is made smooth with the help of buffing machines.

claims.text: The as-cast surface does not take on the decorative patina unless the casting skin is removed.

quotes.quote: the as-cast surface of the metal does not take on the decorative patina if the surface casting skin is not removed.

claims.text: Copper sulphate solution temporarily blackens the smoothed surface so that the design can be seen while it is drawn and engraved.

quotes.quote: The smooth surface is made black temporarily by applying copper sulphate.
Copper sulphate solution is first smea red to the article and this turns the greyish white surface of the alloy-cast article to black.
The surface of the object is made smooth and is darkened temporarily with a solution of copper sulphate; a design is then engraved on the surface to expose the silvery grey of the alloy.
The surface of the object is then blackened with a solution of copper sulphate to allow the artisan to engrave a pattern using chisels and a hammer.

claims.text: Designs are drawn freehand on the metal with a sharp iron point called kalam, and an experienced worker usually needs no replica to copy.

quotes.quote: Only a simple scale and a sharp end of an iron spoke called kalam are used for the purpose.
Usually an experienced worker needs no replica of the proposed design from which he has to copy.

claims.text: Engraving to the required depth, locally called khodna, is done with fine pointed chisels struck with a hammer.

quotes.quote: With finer pointed chisels engraving in the required depth is now carried on.
The operation is called in the local verna cular as khodna.
The chisel is held in the left hand and the hammer in the right hand.

claims.text: During engraving the piece is held fixed in a bed of melted wax mixed with ash or sawdust.

quotes.quote: only possible by embedding it on a wax surface
For preparing such surface, wax is melted thick on a charcoal oven and some ash or saw dust is added to it.

claims.text: Bidri chisels include a needle-sharp drawing kalam for sketching the design and the chilne-ki-kalam, a chisel for chasing.

quotes.quote: (a) drawing kalam or pen with a sharp end like a needle, used to sketch the design on the surface; (b) chilne-ki-kalam Or chisel for chasing

claims.text: Silver bars are made into wire or sheet by a goldsmith and then thinned further by the bidri workers themselves.

quotes.quote: The bars of silver purchased in the market are given to goldsmith to make it into the form of a wire or sheet
that wire or sheet is made further thinner and thinner according to the requirements at the workshOps by the workers themselves

claims.text: Silver wire is thinned by drawing it through the pautha or tarpatti, a steel plate with diamond-drilled holes of different sizes.

quotes.quote: For thinning the wire, it is drawn through the pautha (a steel plate with diamond-drilled holes of different sizes).
The pautha or tarpatti which is about 8" in }ength, is held in posi" tion between the two feet of the worker

claims.text: Embedding the silver wire, called bithana, is done by holding the wire on the engraved design with a flat chisel and hammering it in.

quotes.quote: This is called bithana (to make sit or fix) in vernacular.
The wire is held fast on the engraved design by a flat pointed chisel grasped by the craftsman with left hand, and by the right hand it is hammered into the interstices
chappat ka lam-chisel with a blunt Or :flat end used for embedd,. ing the silver wire into the furrows of the engraved designs

claims.text: In tarkashi and tainishan work the inlaid surface is then filed or sanded level, and the temporary black vanishes to leave a smooth, zinc-white surface.

quotes.quote: filing the above piece with a flat iron file so that the embedded silver and the base material's surface form a smooth single level
This is done only in the case of tarkashi and taihnishan techniques.
the whole surface is again rubbed with sand paper or buffrng machine. Thereafter the temporary black colour vanishes and the surface becomes smooth and zinc-white.

claims.text: The finished article is dipped in a boiling solution of fort earth and ammonium chloride, which turns the zinc alloy black while the silver keeps its colour.

quotes.quote: The polished article is then dipped in a boiled solution of ammonium chloride and earth collected and available only from the fort area
By this process, the zinc portion ofthe articles become black and the silver portion retains its own colour.
The finished article is now given a dip in this hot solution.
The zinc alloy turns permanently jet black while the silver retains its brilliance.

claims.text: Ammonium chloride or sal ammoniac, locally called navsadar, and fort clay are mixed in water in a ratio of 5 to 30 for the blackening bath.

quotes.quote: For blackening the base material saltpetre containing clay and sal ammoniac are mixed in sufficient water in the ratio of 30 : 5
ammonium chloride (locally called as Navsadar) and Bidar fort clay (sieved for granular uniformity and removal of foreign elements) are blended in water in the ratio of 5:30

claims.text: The blackening slurry is boiled in an open iron or aluminium vessel and the engraved piece is rolled in it.

quotes.quote: the poultice is boiled in an open iron or aluminium vessel (Fig. 3b).
the engraved artefact (Fig. 3c) is introduced into the boiling slurry and rolled.

claims.text: Rolla and colleagues report that the engraved piece goes into the slurry when the solution reaches 110-150°C.

quotes.quote: When the solution attains a temperature of 110-150°C, the engraved artefact (Fig. 3c) is introduced into the boiling slurry and rolled.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis reports that artisans heat their sand and ammonium chloride mixture to approximately 80 degrees before dipping the piece.

quotes.quote: In normal practice the artisans use a sand and ammonium chloride mixture. This is heated to approximately 80oC following which the sample is dipped in it.

claims.text: After the dip the article is taken out of the solution and dried for five to ten minutes.

quotes.quote: The article is taken out from the solution and dried for five to ten minutes.

claims.text: The blackened piece is polished with groundnut oil, in some accounts as a paste with fine charcoal powder, to give it a shine.

quotes.quote: Later the whole surface is rubbed with groundnut oil, so as to give the article a shining.
For this purpose a paste of fine charcoal powder and ground nut oil is prepared.
Following this, the object is polished with groundnut oil and charcoal.

claims.text: Oil rubbed into the piece after the mud paste is removed deepens the black hue.

quotes.quote: The mud is removed, and finally oil is rubbed into the piece to deepen the black hue.
After removal of the mud paste, the surface of the piece would be rubbed with oil.

claims.text: The bidri base alloy is 16 parts zinc to one part copper, a proportion of 94 to 6.

quotes.quote: Zinc and copper mixed in the proportion 16 : 1 form the base material for all the articles.
The alloy is composed of 16 parts of zinc and one part of copper or a proportion of 94: 6.
Bidriware is manufactured from an alloy of copper and zinc (in the ratio 1:16) by casting.
copper and zinc are melted in the proportion of I to 16 in a crucible

claims.text: One bidri artisan told The News Minute that 60 gm of copper goes into every kilogram of zinc to get the perfect black hue.

quotes.quote: explains Khwaja, a Bidri artisan
For every kilogram of zinc, we use 60 gm of copper for it to get the perfect black hue.

claims.text: Analysed bidri vessels are zinc alloys with between 2% and 10% copper, the majority between 2% and 5%.

quotes.quote: A number of vessels were analyzed, and all were found to be alloys of zinc with between 2% and 10% copper
They are usually high zinc alloys with between 2 and 10% copper, with the majority between 2 and 5% copper.

claims.text: Lead, tin or iron are present in some bidri alloys, in which zinc predominates.

quotes.quote: Some have lead, tin, or iron also present in the alloy.
Bidri objects are cast from an alloy in which zinc predominates, though small amounts of lead, copper and tin may also be found.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis says lead, tin and iron do not appear consistently in bidri alloys and are probably accidental ingredients.

quotes.quote: Lead, tin and iron are sometimes mentioned in the literature, but do not appear consistently and are probably accidental ingredients.

claims.text: The 1908 Imperial Gazetteer, quoted in the census monograph, melts copper, lead and tin together and adds sixteen ounces of zinc to every three ounces of that alloy.

quotes.quote: extract from the Imperial Ga zetteer of India published in 1908

Its component parts are copper sixteen ounces, lead four ounces and tin two ounces which are melted together,and to every three ounces of the alloy, sixteen ounces ofspeiter, that is of zinc, are added

claims.text: Experienced bidri workers told the census survey that no metal other than zinc and copper is used in the base alloy.

quotes.quote: But the workers including very old people, who have had very long experience, em phasise the fact that no other metal, except zinc and copper, is used for the alloy of the base article.

claims.text: Silver remains the main inlay metal, though brass was used in Deccan bidri until the eighteenth century.

quotes.quote: Silver remains the material of choice for inlay work, though brass was used in Deccan bidriware until the eighteenth century.

claims.text: Jagdish Mittal says early bidris inlaid with two metals were never made after 1725, because brass was a hard metal and slow to work.

quotes.quote: early bidris of two metals were never made after 1725, the reason being that brass is a hard metal and it took more time to work on.

claims.text: The census monograph found gold inlay still practised but rarely used, owing to the scarcity and cost of gold.

quotes.quote: The gold inlay work is still there, but it is rarely used owing to its scarcity and cost.

claims.text: The census monograph reproduces quality-marking standards set for Bidriware at Hyderabad, requiring a base alloy of 93% to 94% zinc and 6% to 7% copper and inlay silver of at least 96%.

quotes.quote: a quality marking scheme was introduced in the State first on a voluntary basis in 1960
The scheme was extended by phases to the other crafts also, including Bidriware at Hyderabad.
Those set up for Bidriware are reproduced below: 1. Base alloy should have the following com position: Zinc = 93% to 94% Copper = 6% to 7%
Silver used for inlay work shOUld contain a minimum of 96% silver

claims.text: The census monograph lists five varieties of bidri work: tarkashi, tainishan, zarnishan in low relief, zarbuland in high relief and aftabi.

quotes.quote: The varieties of workmanship of the designs consist of tarkashi (inlay of wire), tainishan (inlay of sheet), zarnishan (low relief), zarbuland (high relief) and aftabi (cut out designs on overlaid metal sheet).

claims.text: Tarkashi is plain wire inlay, set into grooves made in the surface of the object for the design.

quotes.quote: Tarkashi is nothing but plain wire work. Grooves for the required design are made on the surface of the object.
Tarkashi is simply plain wire work and thus appears to be more intricate with fine lines.

claims.text: Teh nashin is a thick inlay of gold or silver in deep engravings, set flush with the surface without relief.

quotes.quote: Teh nashin refers to 'thick inlay of gold or silver in deep engravings on a baser metal surface' (Sen 1983:37).
The designs are flushed with the surface of the metal without any relief.

claims.text: In aftabi or mehatabi work the silver covers the background while the design appears in black.

quotes.quote: Aftabi, also known as mehatabi, refers to silver inlay on the background while the designs appear to be in black.
The Aftabi also known as Mehatabi work refers to pieces that portray a reversal - the silver seems to form the base while the designs seems to be in black.

claims.text: In zar buland work silver is laid over a lead pad so that the pattern stands up from the surface.

quotes.quote: In bidri it is done using a 'zar buland' where silver is inlaid over a lead pad so that the pattern stands up from the surface (Stronge 1985:11).
In the zarbuland technique, the silver is inlaid over a lead pad and is then incised with motifs or gold overlay, leading to a high-relief effect.
The margin or rim of each is bent over and the cavity thus formed is filled with a piece of soft lead.

claims.text: The zarbuland high-relief inlay style was developed in Lucknow.

quotes.quote: A distinctive inlay style, called zarbuland (high-relief inlaying), was developed in Lucknow.
The inlay with high relief-zarbuland or zarnishan (creating a raised effect)-comes from Lucknow.

claims.text: Ganga-Yamuna work sets gold and silver side by side, though it is now taken to mean an inlay of two or more metals.

quotes.quote: Ganga-Yamuna style - where gold and silver are used side-by-side for inlays, though this is now taken to mean an inlay of two or more metals
The pattern's true meaning of using two specified metals-gold and silver, today translates to the use of any two or more metals for inlay.

claims.text: In Ganga-Yamuna work the gold is inlaid only after the final colouring, because the softer gold tends to fall out during buffing and polishing.

quotes.quote: And after the final colouring of the article, gold is inlaid. This is because gold is a softer metal and it tends to fall out during the process of buffing and polishing.

claims.text: Phooljhadi, also called star work, is the most famous tarkashi design.

quotes.quote: The most famous of Tarkashi designs is Phooljhadi (fountain).
Star work, commonly known as phooljhadi work, is also an example of tarkashi.

claims.text: The Mughal poppy flower motif, said to have been introduced around 1740, was used extensively in eighteenth-century bidri.

quotes.quote: The most beautiful and best known pattern, the 'Mughal poppy flower motif' is said to be introduced around 1740 and has since been used in bidri extensively.
In the eighteenth century, a popular motif, also derived from Mughal art, was the poppy flower, which was used extensively.

claims.text: By the mid-nineteenth century, as the poppy motif declined, the kothmir or coriander leaf motif became popular and lasted into the twentieth century.

quotes.quote: By the mid-nineteenth century, as the quality and use of the poppy motif declined, the kothmir (coriander) leaf motif became popular, and its variations were used until the twentieth century.
The kothmiri design which is seen 1850 onwards, appears to get more prominent and continues until the 20th century.

claims.text: Patterns such as ashrafi-ki booti, teenpatti-ki-booti, stars, vine creepers and the stylised poppy plant are traced back to Persian influence.

quotes.quote: Highly conventionalised patterns, ashrafi-ki booti or teenpatti-ki-booti, stars, vine creepers and stylized poppy plant with flower, single bloom or whole plant in various shapes, mostly in medallion form or mango shape, are amongst those which can be traced back to Persian influence.

claims.text: Fish-shaped spice boxes are common to Lucknow and Bidar, but articles ornamented with fish designs are special to Lucknow.

quotes.quote: Fish-shaped spice boxes are common to Lucknow and Bidar, but articles ornamented with fish designs are special to Lucknow only.
In Lucknow, the double-fish insignia of the Nawabs of Awadh was a common motif.

claims.text: Purnia bidri had two grades by finish, the superior gharki bidri and the inferior karna bidri.

quotes.quote: had two categories of bidriware according to the finish - gharki bidri (superior) and karna bidri (inferior).
Bidri at Purnea was expensive to produce and hence we see two types here-gharki bidri (well-finished) and karna bidri (inferior in finish).

claims.text: Earlier bidri objects included hookah bases, bowls, ewers, betel-leaf boxes, spittoons, cot legs, candelabra, incense burners and rosewater sprinklers.

quotes.quote: Earlier, the technique was used to embellish objects such as hookah base, abkhora or katora (bowl), aftaba (ewer), pandan or khasdan (box for betel leaves), ugaldan (spittoon), palang pae (cot legs), shamadan (candelabra), uddan (incense burner), gulab pash (rosewater sprinkler)

claims.text: In the colonial period bidri was applied to new objects such as flower vases, picture frames, chairs, buttons, walking sticks and cigar boxes.

quotes.quote: In the colonial period, the technique began to be applied to large flower vases and basins, mirror and picture frames, chairs, buttons, walking sticks, cigar boxes and ink stands.

claims.text: The census monograph found decorative motifs from the Ajanta murals used in designing new bidri ware.

quotes.quote: With the increase of interest in the Ajanta murals, many of their decorative motifs found their way in the designing of new fashioned Bidriware

claims.text: Motifs from bidri shown at the Great Exhibition and the Paris exhibition were reproduced by Owen Jones in his book The Grammar of Ornament.

quotes.quote: Bidri ware found a vastly increased market after being shown at the Great Exhibition and the International Exhibition in Paris in 1855.
Motifs drawn from the bidri shown at both exhibitions were reproduced by the British architect and designer Owen Jones (1809-1874) in his book The Grammar of Ornament.

claims.text: To cut production time and labour costs, bidri artisans have turned to tarkashi wire work and screen-printed designs.

quotes.quote: Faced with these issues, bidriware artisans have switched to using tarkashi and screen printing designs in order to cut down on production time and labour costs.
Bidri articles today mostly have wire work, not just in order to cut down the cost but also to reduce time while filling space at the same time.

claims.text: The blackening uses soil from around Bidar fort, which sources describe as found only there and as having oxidising properties.

quotes.quote: It is then dipoed in a solution orepared with the Soil available onlv around the Bidar fort, which has oxidizing properties.
This type of earth needed' which is available qly in the Bidar fort area, has a fine effect on zinc alloy.
The traditional patination process uses the soil from beneath the mud-brick walls of the fort of Bidar city which is said to have special oxidizing properties.
A special earth, found only near Bidar Fort, brews a magical solution
the handicraft mandates the use of Bidar Fort (in Karnataka, India) clay, which bestows the handicraft its characteristic matt-black patina

claims.text: The census monograph says the special clay is found at Bidar only in the ruins of the fort and its walls and in old buildings built with mud only, and is believed to contain saltpetre.

quotes.quote: The special type clay. contain ing saltpetre, is available at Bidar only in the ruins of the fort and walls there, as well as some old buildings which were constructed in those old days with mud only.
It is believed that clay contains saltpetre.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis says the fort soil matters because it is saturated with salts and rich in nitrate, the walls being commonly used as a latrine.

quotes.quote: The main significance of the soil around the fort used in the traditional recipes is that it is saturated with salts because the walls are commonly used as a latrine.
The sand is rich in nitrate due to there being a latrine nearby.

claims.text: Analysis of unused Bidar fort clay found silica, aluminium, magnesium, iron, antimony, carbon and sulphur in elemental and oxide forms.

quotes.quote: The energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis (Fig. 8) report of unused clay contains silica, aluminium, magnesium, iron, antimony, carbon and sulphur in their elemental and oxide forms.

claims.text: Bidar fort clay was found distinct in containing chloride and rare minerals such as antimony, indium and barium, and richer than general soils in calcium, iron, magnesium and carbon.

quotes.quote: the clay sample was distinct on parameters of presence of chloride and rare minerals like antimony, indium, barium and traces of gold
when compared with broad (general) soil compositions, the Bidar fort clay was rich in calcium, iron, magnesium, and carbon

claims.text: Bidar fort soil can be used 3-4 times, depending on the size of the pieces and the time since it was quarried, before it loses its ability to blacken.

quotes.quote: It could be noted here that Bidar fort soil, can be used for 3-4 times,
conditional to the size of the artefact oxidized (patinated), and the time-lag from the period of soil quarrying.
It was recognized that the Bidar fort clay loses its ability to bestow the black sheen (i.e., oxidize) after a few uses (Fig. 7).

claims.text: One bidri artisan told The News Minute that the soil is brought from Bidar fort and tasted to judge whether it is fit for use.

quotes.quote: Two Bidri artisans speak to TNM
The soil is brought from Bidar fort, no other soil will work as perfectly as this one.
We taste the soil to determine if it's fit for use or not

claims.text: The blackening paste is described as mud mixed with ammonium chloride, potassium nitrate and salt, and in one account copper sulphate.

quotes.quote: the craftsman briefly covers the object with a mud paste contining salt, ammonium chloride and unrefined potassium nitrate
This is done by applying a paste of mud mixed with ammonium chloride, potassium nitrate, sodium chloride and copper sulphate.
it is treated with a solution of clay that contains saltpetre, sal ammoniac, sodium chloride and other chemicals

claims.text: La Niece and Martin found that the black patina forms instantly when the alloy is immersed in a warm solution of one part potassium nitrate to four parts ammonium chloride.

quotes.quote: The black patina forms instantaneously on immersion of the alloy in a warm solution of potassium nitrate (one part) and ammonium chloride (four parts).

claims.text: Replication experiments showed that the copper content of the alloy is critical: the patina forms on zinc with 2-10% copper but not on pure zinc or on brass.

quotes.quote: x-ray fluorescence (XRF) analysis and replication experiments have proved that the copper content of the alloy is critical for the patina formation

The patina is easy to produce in the laboratory on alloys of zinc with 2-10% copper, falling within the ε + η phase field of the binary copper-zinc equilibrium diagram, but it does not form on pure zinc or on brass
Standard brasses, as used for the inlay, are unaffected by the solution which induces only a whitish-gray patina on pure zinc.

claims.text: Ammonium chloride preferentially dissolves zinc from the bidri alloy, leaving a copper-enriched surface.

quotes.quote: The ammonium chloride preferentially dissolves the zinc from the Bidri alloy.
In such a solution zinc dissolves preferentially leading to copper enriched surface

claims.text: La Niece and Martin suggested, while calling it unproven, that the copper-enriched surface is then oxidised by potassium nitrate.

quotes.quote: The rest of the process is unproven but it is suggested that the resulting copper-enriched surface is oxidized by potassium nitrate.

claims.text: La Niece and Martin reported that the compounds forming the black patina had not been identified, and a V&A record calls the exact chemical process still unidentified.

quotes.quote: The compound or compounds forming the patina have not been identified.
The exact chemical process which takes place is still unidentified.

claims.text: None of the commonly occurring zinc compounds is black, and La Niece wrote that no adequate explanation for the patina's colour had yet been published.

quotes.quote: None of the commonly occurring zinc compounds is black and no adequate explanation for the colour of the patina has yet been published.
as technically, none of the zinc compounds are black in colour

claims.text: La Niece proposes that the patina looks matt black because its small, acicular particles absorb light, rather than because of additional components.

quotes.quote: it is now proposed that it is the ability of the patina particles, by reason of their small size and acicular form, to absorb light which gives the appearance of a matt black surface, rather than the existence of additional components within the patina.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis inferred that the copper-enriched surface converts in nitrate solution to CuO and Cu2O, and that these oxides give the black appearance.

quotes.quote: From the current investigation, the following can be inferred
In such a solution zinc dissolves preferentially leading to copper enriched surface, which in nitrate containing solution converts to CuO and Cu2O. These oxides render the black appearance.

claims.text: X-ray diffraction of bidri patinas found simonkolleite, zincite and cuprite as the main crystalline phases, which are white or reddish rather than black.

quotes.quote: identified the three main crystalline components of all the object and experimental patinas analysed:- Simonkolleite, zinc hydroxychloride (Zn5(OH)8 Cl2) Zincite, zinc oxide (ZnO) Cuprite, copper I oxide (Cu2O)
The two zinc compounds identified are white in colour and cuprite appears reddish, so these results do not directly explain the black colouration of the patina.

claims.text: Black copper II oxide, tenorite, had been expected in the bidri patina but was only rarely found.

quotes.quote: The copper II oxide tenorite (CuO) does appear black, and had been expected to be present, but it was only rarely found in the patina

claims.text: An experimental patina on a specially prepared zinc alloy with about 4% copper measured only about three to ten micrometres thick in cross-section.

quotes.quote: Similar experiments were performed with a specially prepared alloy of zinc containing 4% copper.
To provide more information, the experimental patina was examined using FE SEMEDX.
The depth of the patina was measured in cross- section using the SEM and found to be only of the order of three to ten micrometres thick.
The alloy composition of the unpatinated surface is approximately 4% copper and 96% zinc.

claims.text: The bidri surface is described as a network of copper-rich dendrites, which in an experimental patina held 12-30% copper against 2-5% in the interdendritic phase.

quotes.quote: To provide more information, the experimental patina was examined using FE SEMEDX.
In the patinated area the dendrites were found to contain 12-30% copper and the interdendritic phase 2-5% copper.
The current manuscript brings to focal the characterization of the Bidri surface that is a dense network of dendrites and inter-dendrites perforations, with copper-rich surfaces

claims.text: ED-XRF analysis of a patinated bidri surface measured 91.681% zinc and 6.110% copper, with traces of sulphur, potassium, calcium and iron.

quotes.quote: Elements Zn Cu S K Ca Fe Composition (in %) 91.681 6.110 1.046 0.676 0.478 0.009
which exhibited existence of the fundamental alloys; besides traces of sulphur, potassium, calcium and iron

claims.text: The black patina is credited with protecting bidri ware from corrosion under normal atmospheric conditions.

quotes.quote: A lot of this anti-corrosive characteristics has been attributed to the black patina that is formed.
The black patina on bidri ware also seems to protect it from unattractive corrosion growths under a range of normal atmospheric conditions.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis found that 20 g of ammonium chloride and 5 g of potassium nitrate in 100 ml of water gave a black patina like that from Bidri sand.

quotes.quote: 5g of potassium nitrate (KNO3), 20g of ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) was dissolved in 100 ml of de-ionised water
An alternative to Bidri sand has been identified. A mixture of NH4Cl and KNO3 (20g:5g) in 100mL of de-ionized water renders black patina on the surface similar to one seen with Bidri sand.

claims.text: An IIT Madras thesis suggests the clay could merely supply nitrate and act as a poultice absorbing the unwanted zinc chloride formed.

quotes.quote: The use of clay does not seem to be crucially important. It could merely serve as a source of alkali nitrate and as a poultice to absorb the unwanted zinc chloride formed during the process.

lede.text: Bidriware is a metal craft of Bidar in which designs engraved on a cast zinc-copper alloy are inlaid with silver, a kind of damascene work.
It takes its name from the city of Bidar, where the technique is thought to have originated, and Bidar and Hyderabad are named as its chief centres of production.
A dip in a boiling solution of fort earth and ammonium chloride turns the zinc alloy black while the silver keeps its colour, and the black background contrasts strikingly with the lustrous inlay.
An IIT Madras thesis says the craft has been handed down mostly among the local Muslim and Lingayat communities.

sentences.text: Sources differ on when bidri began at Bidar: the GI application dates it both to the reign of Ahmed Shah Bahamani (1422 to 1436) and to about 400 years ago, while a craftsman's account in the census monograph credits Allauddin II with inviting the craftsmen of Bijapur to Bidar.
The V&A dates surviving pieces to the late 16th or early 17th century, while Sahapedia notes that no examples from the 15th or 16th centuries have been found in paintings or literature.

The Impart encyclopedia names a Deccani painting of about 1625 showing a bidri hookah as the earliest evidence, and Jagdish Mittal identifies the earliest written reference to bidri ware in Chahar Gulshan, written in 1759.

The Impart encyclopedia says bidri had spread to the courts of Purnia and Murshidabad by the late eighteenth century and to Lucknow by the nineteenth, while Sahapedia dates production there to the early 19th century.

Bidri flourished under the Asaf Jahi rulers, many artisans from Bidar migrated to Hyderabad, and the census monograph records a further migration in 1956 and 1957 after Bidar was placed in Mysore State.
Bidriware was exhibited at the Great Exhibition of 1851 and the Exposition Universelle of 1855, and the exhibitions stimulated demand but led to repetitious designs and inferior quality.

The GI application's method of production runs from melting and casting the alloy through smoothing, temporary blackening, engraving, silver inlay and sanding to dipping in fort earth solution, drying and oiling.
The alloy is melted in a crucible in a furnace that uses coal, the zinc first and the copper then added.
Moulds are made in hollow iron frames called darza boxes, with a thin layer of fine red clay mixed with resin and castor oil over the pattern and ordinary red clay filling the rest.
The cast article is smoothed on a lathe and with files, and copper sulphate solution temporarily blackens the surface so that the design can be seen while it is drawn and engraved.
Designs are drawn freehand with a sharp iron point called kalam and engraved with fine pointed chisels struck with a hammer.
Silver wire drawn thin through the pautha is hammered into the engraved design, and in tarkashi and tainishan work the surface is then filed or sanded level.
The finished article is dipped in a boiling solution of fort earth and ammonium chloride, dried for five to ten minutes and polished with groundnut oil.
The blackening paste is described as mud mixed with ammonium chloride, potassium nitrate and salt, and the black patina forms instantly in a warm solution of potassium nitrate and ammonium chloride.
Ammonium chloride preferentially dissolves zinc from the bidri alloy, leaving a copper-enriched surface.
The copper content of the alloy is critical: the patina forms on zinc with 2-10% copper but not on pure zinc or on brass.
La Niece and Martin reported that the compounds forming the black patina had not been identified, and none of the commonly occurring zinc compounds is black.
Sources differ on the colour: an IIT Madras thesis inferred that copper oxides give the black appearance, while X-ray diffraction found white or reddish phases and only rarely black tenorite.
An experimental patina measured only about three to ten micrometres thick, and the black patina is credited with protecting bidri ware from corrosion.
The base alloy is 16 parts zinc to one part copper, a proportion of 94 to 6, and analysed vessels are zinc alloys with between 2% and 10% copper.
Sources differ on lead and tin: the 1908 Imperial Gazetteer melts copper, lead and tin into the alloy, while experienced workers said no metal other than zinc and copper is used.
Silver remains the main inlay metal, though brass was used in Deccan bidri until the eighteenth century, and the census monograph found gold inlay rarely used owing to its scarcity and cost.
The census monograph reproduces quality-marking standards set for Bidriware at Hyderabad, requiring 93% to 94% zinc and 6% to 7% copper in the base alloy and at least 96% silver in the inlay.
The blackening uses soil from around Bidar fort, which sources describe as having oxidising properties.
Sources differ on where the clay is found: around the fort only, or, as the census monograph says, also in old buildings built with mud, and it is believed to contain saltpetre.
Unused Bidar fort clay contains silica, aluminium, magnesium, iron, antimony, carbon and sulphur, and is richer than general soils in calcium, iron, magnesium and carbon.
Bidar fort soil can be used for 3-4 times before it loses its ability to give the black sheen.

Sources group bidri inlay differently: the census monograph lists tarkashi, tainishan, zarnishan in low relief, zarbuland in high relief and aftabi, while the GI application and Sahapedia treat zar buland and zar nashin as one kind.
Tarkashi is plain wire inlay, teh nashin a thick inlay flush with the surface, and in aftabi work the silver covers the background while the design appears in black.
In zar buland work silver is laid over a lead pad so that the pattern stands up from the surface, a high-relief style developed in Lucknow.
The Mughal poppy flower motif, said to have been introduced around 1740, was used extensively in eighteenth-century bidri, and by the mid-nineteenth century the kothmir leaf motif became popular.
In the colonial period bidri was applied to new objects such as flower vases, picture frames, buttons and cigar boxes.
Bidriware is a registered geographical indication under application number 20, filed by the Karnataka State Handicrafts Development Corporation Limited on 24 January 2005.
The registry issued certificate number 21 on 30 January 2006, while Sahapedia gives the beginning of 2008 as the date of the tag.

The GI application, filed in 2005, put the number of artisans at Bidar at about 500, and the census monograph, whose survey day was 24 February 1966, puts the craft there at 61 households and 96 workers.
The census monograph estimated that about 25% of production cost went to raw materials and about 75% to wages and sundry items.
The industry faces the high cost of and access to silver and saltpetre-bearing clay, poorly remunerated artisans and counterfeit bidriware.
